case_study_insert.main_stem: Willowbrook Early Learning (WEL) is a private limited company in the early-years childcare sector, based in the Toronto region and running nursery centres, employing a workforce of 65. Founded in 2013 by Nadia Farouk, it works with local parent groups and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. WEL plans to invest $780,000 in a new nursery wing with outdoor learning areas and recycled-fibre play equipment, financed by a $480,000 ten-year bank loan, $250,000 retained profit and a $50,000 overdraft. It has fixed costs of $288,000 a year, a variable cost of $12 a unit and a selling price of $30, and produces 45,000 units a year. WEL faces an attendance-recording error rate of 6.8% and nursery-worker absenteeism of 13%.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Operations Log — Q4 2025: The nurseries recorded 10,500 child-place weeks last quarter with an attendance-recording error rate of 6.8%, down from 9.1% a year earlier. Parent complaints fell from 52 to 28 a month. Average settling-in period is 12.4 days. A survey of 380 parents found 79% would pay $18 more a week for outdoor learning, and 68% check staff-to-child ratios before enrolling. A skills audit shows 22 of 65 nursery workers have not completed on-the-job training on the new safeguarding app; off-the-job training courses in childcare at the city college cost $580 per worker.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Willowbrook Early Learning for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Childcare Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.00% to 4.75%, increasing the cost of variable-rate borrowing. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 7.4% from $13.50 to $14.50 per hour from April 2026, lifting nursery-worker payroll costs. (3) Outdoor play equipment and recycled-fibre input costs have risen 9.3% year-on-year, while demand for early-years places grew 3.9%.

questions.question_text: WEL is funding part of its $780,000 nursery wing with a $480,000 ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for WEL of using the $250,000 retained profit instead of borrowing more.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit has no interest charge or repayment schedule, so WEL protects the cash flow needed to meet fixed costs of $288,000 a year while it services the $480,000 loan and the $50,000 overdraft. Every dollar not paid to the bank can absorb the 9.3% rise in outdoor-equipment costs, helping WEL hold its $30 selling price for the local parent groups it works with.

Point 2: Using $250,000 retained profit keeps Nadia Farouk's ownership intact and avoids further collateral risk. The $780,000 wing cannot be repossessed if enrolments fall short of the 45,000 units, and the survey showing 79% of 380 parents would pay $18 more a week for outdoor learning gives WEL grounds to fund the launch from its own resources rather than increase borrowing. With 13% absence and a 6.8% recording error rate already straining the nurseries, keeping cash free of interest matters more than adding another fixed repayment; it also leaves the $50,000 overdraft as a short-term buffer rather than permanent debt.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to WEL's financing decision and its nursery operations.

questions.question_text: WEL is promoting its new outdoor-learning nursery wing. Consider local parent-group advertising, nursery open days, or social media campaigns. Which should WEL choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Local parent-group advertising: Leaflets and notices through the local parent groups WEL already works with can announce the $780,000 wing cheaply across the Toronto region. This reaches families directly and is affordable for a business with a $480,000 loan and a $50,000 overdraft, but print is passive, cannot show the outdoor learning areas or recycled-fibre equipment, and may be discarded before the 10,500 child-place weeks recorded last quarter need filling.

Nursery open days: Inviting parents to visit the wing lets them see the outdoor areas and ask about staff-to-child ratios, which matters because 68% of 380 surveyed parents check those ratios before enrolling. Open days also demonstrate the premium service wanted by the 79% who would pay $18 more a week, cost little beyond staff time, and build trust through WEL's existing parent-group links. They reach fewer people than advertising and need careful timing around a 12.4-day settling-in period, but the trust and enrolment conversion are higher.

Social media campaigns: Targeted posts can show children using the new equipment and measure enquiries against the 6.8% attendance-recording error rate and 12.4-day settling-in period. They are cheap and fast, but childcare decisions depend on confidence in staff, so online interest may not convert into places without a visit.

Recommendation: WEL should choose nursery open days, supported by parent-group notices. Open days are low-cost, show the facilities directly and match the 68% who check ratios. Parent-group advertising alone is rejected as passive and unable to answer questions; social media is rejected because it cannot build the trust needed for a 13%-absence-sensitive service as effectively as a face-to-face visit.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal application to WEL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of WEL with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of WEL with a well-justified recommendation explaining why parent-group advertising and social media are rejected.

questions.question_text: WEL's attendance-recording error rate is 6.8% and nursery-worker absenteeism 13%. Explain two benefits for WEL of using democratic leadership with its workforce of 65.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership invites the 65 nursery workers to suggest how the new safeguarding app should be used, which suits WEL's hierarchical structure when records must be accurate. Staff who help design the recording routine are more likely to follow it, pushing the 6.8% error rate below last year's 9.1% and protecting the 10,500 child-place weeks recorded last quarter and the 68% of parents who check staff-to-child ratios.

Point 2: Consultation raises job satisfaction and reduces 13% absence, because workers who are listened to are more committed to their shifts. Better attendance shortens the 12.4-day settling-in period for new children and cuts the need to retrain the 22 of 65 workers missing on-the-job training at $580 each, protecting the return on the $780,000 wing. In a hierarchical structure the workers closest to the app and the daily registers can spot where errors enter the system and propose fixes managers would miss, while the $580 college fee can be spent on new qualifications rather than basic familiarisation.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to WEL's error rate, absence, training and expansion.

questions.question_text: WEL must train 22 of 65 nursery workers who have not completed on-the-job training on the new safeguarding app. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the city college. Which should WEL choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching on the actual safeguarding app is specific to WEL's own recording routines and costs no course fees, while the 22 trainees continue to cover the 10,500 child-place weeks from last quarter. Supervisors can correct entries immediately, the fastest way to reduce the 6.8% attendance-recording error rate below 9.1%. Drawbacks are that senior staff lose time from their own duties, local shortcuts may spread, and there is no external certificate for parents who check staff-to-child ratios.

Off-the-job training: The city college childcare course at $580 per worker costs 22 × $580 = $12,760, modest beside the $780,000 wing. It gives structured safeguarding knowledge and a recognised certificate that can reassure the 68% of parents who check ratios. However, it removes 22 of 65 nursery workers from the centres, which could lengthen the 12.4-day settling-in period and worsen 13% absence, and generic teaching still needs adapting to WEL's app.

Decision: WEL should choose on-the-job training first, with a short certified college module later for senior workers. On-the-job coaching is cheaper, app-specific and avoids reducing nursery cover while absence is 13%. Full off-the-job training is rejected now because removing 22 of 65 workers would disrupt the 10,500-place schedule and the $12,760 fee is premature before the 6.8% error rate is reduced. With recording errors at 6.8%, correcting entries on the live app gives faster feedback than sample forms in a classroom. WEL should measure that rate after a pilot and reconsider the $12,760 college option only if it has not moved toward last year's 9.1% figure.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to WEL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of both training methods in the context of WEL.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and app relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how WEL's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $288,000 ÷ ($30 − $12) = $288,000 ÷ $18 = 16,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 16,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $30 − $12 = $18. Answer: contribution per unit is $18.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways WEL's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Comparing the 16,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 45,000 units gives a margin of safety of 29,000 units, showing how far enrolments could fall before the wing makes a loss.
2. Contribution per unit of $18 lets managers test pricing: a $2 discount from $30 to $28 leaves $16 contribution, so they can judge whether extra places still cover the $288,000 fixed costs.
3. Knowing fixed costs and contribution helps set the volume needed to service the $480,000 bank loan and $50,000 overdraft, checking the $780,000 wing can meet repayments.
4. Managers can benchmark unit cost, $288,000 ÷ 45,000 units = $6.40 plus $12 = $18.40 a child-place week, across terms to spot the 6.8% recording error rate and 13% absence driving rework.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 16,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $18 | (iii) Four contextual uses: 29,000-unit safety margin against 45,000-unit output; discount pricing from $30 against $18 contribution; loan and overdraft servicing for the $780,000 wing; and unit-cost benchmarking at $18.40 to tackle recording errors.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate WEL's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has WEL's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 45.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 20.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 25.0%
ROCE 2024 = 15.0%
ROCE 2025 = 20.0%

Detailed workings: 2024 gross profit of $540,000 came from $1,350,000 revenue less $810,000 cost of sales, so $540,000 ÷ $1,350,000 × 100 = 40.0. In 2025, $1,620,000 revenue less $891,000 cost of sales gives $729,000, so $729,000 ÷ $1,620,000 × 100 = 45.0. Operating profit of $270,000 in 2024 and $405,000 in 2025 divided by revenue gives $270,000 ÷ $1,350,000 × 100 = 20.0 and $405,000 ÷ $1,620,000 × 100 = 25.0. Returns on capital were $270,000 ÷ $1,800,000 × 100 = 15.0 in 2024 and $405,000 ÷ $2,025,000 × 100 = 20.0 in 2025. Interest payable rose from $40,000 to $50,000, so the gain was not caused by cheaper borrowing.

Evaluation: All three measures improved. The gross margin rose from 40.0% to 45.0% because revenue grew from $1,350,000 to $1,620,000 while cost of sales increased more slowly, so each child-place week retained more after direct costs. The operating margin improved from 20.0% to 25.0%, showing the $288,000 fixed-cost base was covered far better as the wing filled. Returns on capital climbed from 15.0% to 20.0% even though capital employed rose from $1,800,000 to $2,025,000, so the new investment is working. These are operational gains, since operating profit rose despite higher interest payable. The caution is the 6.8% attendance-recording error rate and 13% absence, which could raise costs if the $780,000 wing is not managed well.

Conclusion: WEL's financial performance has improved. The gross margin (40.0% to 45.0%), operating margin (20.0% to 25.0%) and returns on capital (15.0% to 20.0%) all rose together on higher revenue and gross profit, not on accounting effects. WEL should protect the gain by cutting recording errors and absence.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the three margins/return for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of revenue, costs, capital and interest movements and a justified conclusion on whether performance improved.

questions.question_text: WEL is considering installing outdoor learning areas across all its nursery centres. Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for WEL of this decision.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Outdoor learning matches the 79% of 380 surveyed parents who would pay $18 more a week and the 68% who check staff-to-child ratios, helping protect the $18 contribution per unit on 45,000 places and supporting the $780,000 wing investment.

Disadvantage: Building and maintaining outdoor areas raises the $12 variable cost per unit or the fixed-cost base, and the insert gives no figure for the extra cost, so the net effect cannot be quantified honestly. Poor weather or equipment failure would also lengthen the 12.4-day settling-in period and add to the 6.8% attendance-recording error rate before the new wing stabilises. Outdoor areas also give staff a practical way to meet the expectations of the 68% who check staff-to-child ratios, strengthening the case for the $18 weekly premium. No extra cost is provided, so WEL should pilot one centre and compare the 6.8% error rate and 12.4-day settling-in period before equipping every nursery or committing capital beyond the $780,000 wing.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to WEL's survey data, costs and quality record.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 4.75%, the 7.4% minimum wage increase to $14.50 and the 9.3% rise in outdoor equipment and recycled-fibre input costs will affect WEL. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.00% to 4.75%): The increase is 0.75 of a percentage point, so if WEL's $480,000 ten-year loan is variable-rate the extra cost is 0.75% × $480,000 = $3,600 a year (0.0075 × $480,000). The $50,000 overdraft would also become dearer. That is modest beside fixed costs of $288,000, and a fixed-rate loan would avoid it. Higher rates could make future borrowing dearer and slightly dampen the 3.9% growth in demand for early-years places.

Minimum wage increase (7.4%, to $14.50 an hour): WEL's workforce of 65 includes hourly-paid nursery workers, so payroll costs rise and cannot be avoided. The insert gives neither hours worked nor individual pay, so an annual wage total would be invented. The defensible test is productivity: 45,000 units ÷ 65 staff = 692.3 child-place weeks per worker, so the higher wage is affordable only if that rate holds or improves; cutting 13% absence and the 6.8% error rate and training the 22 untrained workers can help sustain it.

Input cost inflation (9.3%): Outdoor equipment and recycled-fibre materials feed the $12 variable cost on each place. The insert does not decompose that cost, so only a bound is honest: if the whole $12 were exposed, 9.3% × $12 = $1.116 per unit, and at 45,000 units that is 45,000 × $1.116 = $50,220 a year. Even a smaller exposed share would erode the $18 contribution on every place sold.

Conclusion: The 9.3% rise in outdoor equipment and recycled-fibre costs will have the greatest impact. It repeats across all 45,000 places and directly attacks the $18 contribution that services the $480,000 loan and funds the $780,000 wing, whereas the interest rise costs $3,600 a year and the wage effect can be offset by sustaining 692.3 child-place weeks per worker. WEL should cut the 6.8% error rate and seek the $18 premium rather than absorb the whole increase.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to WEL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on WEL's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in context with a well-justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.
